messages.subject: contrasts in glht
messages.subject_clean: contrasts in glht
messages.body_plain:
Does anyone have any familiarity with combing levels using the glht function within the multcomp package to compare means? The minimal adequate model contains two factors, treatment and temp. Treatment has 3 levels (dry, no, wet) as does temp (10,15,20). I want to conduct pairwise comparisons of  treatment levels as well as combine "dry" and "wet" and compare to the "no" (litter) treatment.  I feel confident that I have the contrast matrix setup correctly for the first 3 comparisons, but am not sure how to combine groups - the combined estimate is way higher than what I calculated by hand, so I'm pretty sure that  doing something wrong. Thanks for the assistance.

Cheers,
Patrick

"no vs dry" = c(0, 0, 0, 1,0),

"wet vs dry" = c(0, 0, 0, 0,1),
"wet + dry vs no" = c(2, 0, 0, -1,-1))#,
comps <- glht(admbm2, contrast.matrix)
summary(comps)

messages.body_plain:
Patrick,

It's been a few days, so maybe you've got this settled. Here's my take (disclaimer: I'm no expert on this stuff)

To combine you need to take an average. Also, the default contrasts in R (as output by summary) are 'treatment contrasts' meaning the non-(Intercept) coefficients are contrasts with the baseline. So:

1. For the combined contrast I think you want:
"wet + dry vs no" = 1/2 * c(0, 0, 0, 1,1))#,

2. for consistent meaning of 'vs' in your contrast names, should you have?
"no vs wet" = c(0, 0, 0, 1,-1),

3. note that because of the coding and treatment contrasts, these comparisons really give the magnitude of the estimated difference at temp10. If you want the average difference across the temperatures, you could change your contrast on temp -- I think this might work:

data$temp <- C(data$temp, contr.helmert)

But, maybe a simpler option is to fit instead without the intercept, i.e.

formula = catsurv.2 ~ -1 + temp + treat ...

In that case you would have to rewrite your contrasts above that involve 'dry' to have a -1 on the appropriate term, and add 1/3 to all temp coefficients.

Hope this helps,
Jaime

messages.subject: post hoc operations on posterior distributions
messages.subject_clean: post hoc operations on posterior distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hi D-RUGers,

I've got what seems like an elemental question/doubt about Bayesian stats that I'm embarrassed to admit I don't know the answer to.

I fitted a Bayesian LMM to plant growth data from several species in 2 conditions (control and cold).  I have posterior distributions of the growth rates (i.e. slopes) for each species derived from the above model.

I want to calculate growth rate difference (control - cold) and relative growth rate (cold / control) from my posterior distributions.  What is the proper way to do so?

1) To simply take the growth rate estimates from the same MCMC iterations and subtract or divide them?

or

2) To randomly sample from the posterior distributions of growth rates before subtracting and dividing them?

I had been doing (1) with the rationale that those are the model's growth rate estimate for iteration-n and should thus be operated on together.  However, I now have a nagging doubt that (2) is the proper way of doing this because it treats the growth rate posteriors as the probability distributions that they are.

What is the proper way to do this?

Thanks!
Dan.

--
Daniel Fulop, Ph.D.
Postdoctoral Scholar
Dept. Plant Biology, UC Davis
Maloof Lab, Rm. 2220
Life Sciences Addition, One Shields Ave.
Davis, CA 95616

Cool. I should have said "may be off". But also want to clarify as I realize now I may have misinterpreted. Sampling is fine, and may be necessary in practice, just sample the same iterations for each parameter. So, what I meant to say is fine is:

- sample the MCMC chain at a set of iterations (put these, say in the cols of at data frame with colnames = your parameters)
- operate on these columnwise to give your output

If (1) actually meant taking the estimates and doing division, then this may give an incorrect answer for the variance unless you are careful to also include the covariance in the formula. It's easier just to sample the same iterations and calculate the quantity on those iterators.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Jaime and Vince.

Vince, I have no [appreciable] autocorrelation in my slope posteriors because they're thinned enough.  You're correct to say that permuting iterations is the safest if there's remaining autocorrelation.  In my case, since I want to keep the total number of samples the same (i.e. 10K), permuting the iterations (i.e. rows of the matrix of posteriors) won't affect the results.

However, if I sample the iterations (rows) *with replacement* then the results will be slightly different due to Monte Carlo error.  Permuting is the same as sampling without replacement...

So, should I sample the iterations with replacement?  ...that seems to be different than what extract.samples() does, though.  Otherwise, since I'm using all iterations I have saved, it doesn't make a difference.

Jaime Ashander wrote:
> Cool. I should have said "may be off". But also want to clarify as I realize now I may have misinterpreted. Sampling is fine, and may be necessary in practice, just sample the same iterations for each parameter. So, what I meant to say is fine is:
>
> - sample the MCMC chain at a set of iterations (put these, say in the cols of at data frame with colnames = your parameters)
> - operate on these columnwise to give your output
>
> If (1) actually meant taking the estimates and doing division, then this may give an incorrect answer for the variance unless you are careful to also include the covariance in the formula. It's easier just to sample the same iterations and calculate the quantity on those iterators.

messages.subject: Correlation study: Seeking advice
messages.subject_clean: Correlation study: Seeking advice
messages.body_plain:
Hello folks!

This is my 1st post here, and its kind of lengthy, sorry! :)
I would consider myself a stats and R newbie, so any help from your group would be greatly appreciated.
Thank you!
Anand

BACKGROUND

I have an observation that I have made regarding a specific class of Transposable Elements (TEs):
For 12 plant species, the number of non-autonomous elements appears to be very highly correlated to autonomous elements. R2~ 0.95

So I process this information further, as follows
I split the sum total of all TEs, both autonomous and non-autonomous into families based on clustering of its 30bp terminal sequences at 80% identity. This resulted in 2709 clusters, that I will call 2709 "families".

Then I counted how many TEs  are in each family for each species and make 2 data grids - one containing counts for just the autonomous TEs, another containing the counts for just the non-autonomous TEs.

Note that TOTAL TEs = autonomous TEs + non-autonomous TEs, for non-biologists in the group.
Also note that majority of the cells in these grids are 0 (zeroes).

I also have versions of these same two data grids where I have converted these counts into Presence / Absence Variation (PAV) i.e 1 vs. 0 grids of numbers.
This is based on simple conversion.
Count = 0, Absence
Count >= 1, Presence

In summary I have 4 data frames
Autonomous TEs in 2709 families, 12 species - count data
Autonomous TEs in 2709 families, 12 species - PAV data
Non-Autonomous TEs in 2709 families, 12 species - count data
Non-Autonomous TEs in 2709 families, 12 species - PAV data

To re-cap, each data grid is 2709 rows * 12 columns
No. of families = 2709
No. of species = 12
and may contain counts, OR PAV data as 0 vs. 1.

BIOLOGICAL QUESTION

What I want to check is whether between these 2 grids, there is a cell to cell correlation. Why? Because I want to test whether the autonomous TE i.e coding for a transposase enzyme, will preferentially or even exclusively amplify only those family members that are most related to it, i.e. in the same family. Why? Because mechanistically transposases recognize terminal sequences, and we know the terminals for this class of TEs are highly divergent in sequence.

So I would expect that because of sequence variation, there would also be variation in transposase specificity.
But I want to test this in a statistically valid manner, which is where I seek your help...

In other words, the high correlation at the coarse "species level" that I observe, I want to test at the finer "family level" both within a species, and across species.

I can do this for all 12 species, or for 1 species, or some number > 1, < 12.

MATH / STATS QUESTIONS

My biological questions translated into math / stats questions:

1. when the count of non-autonomous Helitrons is higher in a family, are there more non-autonomous Helitrons in that family?

2. And conversely, when the count of non-autonomous Helitrons is lower for a family, are there fewer non-autonomous Helitrons in that family?

3. If yes, does it hold true across all species, and across all families, OR
all species, some families, OR
some species, all famiies etc.

(BIOLOGY) HYPOTHESES

My hypothesis is that autonomous TEs act within just their own family to amplify it.

My alternate hypothesis 1 - is that autonomous TEs act across some closely related families to amplify across this subset.
i.e. Some limited specificity of terminal sequence recognition by transposase. And families are related based on similarity of their terminal sequences

My alternate hypothesis 2 - is that autonomous Helitrons across all families and expand them.
i.e. No specificity of terminal sequence recognition by transposase, high promiscuity of amplification of terminals.

HELP / ADVICE I SEEK FROM YOU

1. So how should I go about performing this analysis? Using GLM or something else?

2. Should I use counts to counts comparison for the stats analysis
OR
should I also look at counts <=> PAV, PAV <=> counts, or even PAV <=> PAV comparison, because I can think of ways where it might make sense

3. Does it make sense to analyze just one species at a time? In which case, it will be more or less like an Excel scatter plot with regression line and R2 value on it. Right?

4. OR  should I necessarily use as many species as possible? Is 12 a sufficient number? I can imagine a scenario where one Helitron cluster i.e. one of the 2709 families, shows high correlation between # autonomous and non-autonomous counts, across all 12 species. But is n=12 high enough to provide good p-value stats support for this?

5. I mentioned a LOT of the grid cells are zeroes. So it should be OK to remove cases where both the autonomous and non-autonomous counts = 0, since they should not alter the results, correct?
Other than the obvious scenrario of
# autonomous > 0, # non-autonomous > 0,
you can also imagine cases where:
# autonomous = 0, # non-autonomous > 0, and conversely
# autonomous > 0, # non-autonomous = 0
Therefore, will the analysis have to be performed in a special way to factor in these scenarios?
In that context, does it make sense to also include PAV data for the comparisons?

I will stop here and wait for your suggestions. I am not attaching my data here, but if any of you want to take a peek and play around with it, I'd be happy to share it.

Thank you!
Anand

messages.body_plain:
Hi Anand,

I have an idea for one way in which how you could go about doing such an analysis: zero-inflated poisson or negative binomial GLMM of non-autonomous TE as response (Y) and autonomous as predictor (X), with a TE family random effect.  In R you could use MCMCglmm for that; going bayesian has advantages in terms of family-wise post hoc inference to assess correlation/covariation.  You could also fit such a model with Stan, but the learning curve will be steeper.

However, one question is nagging me... How closely related are your species?  ...because you may want to account for the effect of phylogeny, which MCMCglmm can do.

HTH,
Dan.

Hi Anand,

On second thought, in terms of adjusting for phylogenetic affect, perhaps I should've asked: How old are the 2079 TE families?  Are they homologous, i.e. do they all share a single origin for Eudicots and grasses, etc?

MCMCglmm is a contributed package, not base R.  It has good vignettes and documentation, but the learning curve can be a bit steep in terms of specifying priors  ...although the default priors often work quite well for simple models, which yours would be.

I or others can help with the MCMCglmm model syntax, etc.  I'll try to post an example model call later today or tomorrow.

Another thing to consider in terms of measurement error is how sensitive is your assay for finding TEs, i.e. could some TEs be there in a given species and just not be detected?  ...e.g. because they're in an unassembled part of the genome.

Cheers,
Dan.

Hi again Daniel,

All important questions, please see my responses in-line.

On Mon, Jun 8, 2015 at 5:04 PM, Daniel Fulop <dfulo...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Anand,
>

> On second thought, in terms of adjusting for phylogenetic affect, perhaps I should've asked: How old are the 2079 TE families?  Are they homologous, i.e. do they all share a single origin for Eudicots and grasses, etc?

I have not determined age of TEs,so I do not know the answer to this question. But I can say with reasonable certainty that there is way more stochasticity in the birth and death of TEs - especially non-autonomous, than classic genes for example. But you already know that. This TE class captures genes and gene fragments, which means on top of this stochasticity, is another layer of selection. So while closely related species will have a common origin of a small subset of TEs, I will expect divergence rates to be higher than for regular non-TE genes. At this point, I do not want to go into the annotation of TE contents, and I am happy with classifying them based on their terminal sequences... Does that answer these questions?

MCMCglmm is a contributed package, not base R.  It has good vignettes and documentation, but the learning curve can be a bit steep in terms of specifying priors  ...although the default priors often work quite well for simple models, which yours would be.

Got it. I wonder if you were referring to or thinking about this: http://glmmadmb.r-forge.r-project.org/

I or others can help with the MCMCglmm model syntax, etc.  I'll try to post an example model call later today or tomorrow.

Thanks a lot!

Another thing to consider in terms of measurement error is how sensitive is your assay for finding TEs, i.e. could some TEs be there in a given species and just not be detected?  ...e.g. because they're in an unassembled part of the genome.

That is a very pertinent question. Of course, for relatively less well characterized species - in terms of assembly, prediction, annotation etc., of which there are several in that list of species, there will be chances of missing TEs. Since the number of autonomous TEs can be 1-2 orders of magnitude fewer than for autonomous TEs, I suspect the chance of artifactual counts for autonomous TEs will be be higher than for non-autonomous TEs. Does that logic make sense? And if you agree, does that change anything in your suggestions?

Cheers,
Dan.

> > > all species, some families, OR
> > > some species, all famiies etc.
> > >
> > >
> > > (BIOLOGY) HYPOTHESES
> > >
> > > My hypothesis is that autonomous TEs act within just their own family to amplify it.
> > >
> > > My alternate hypothesis 1 - is that autonomous TEs act across some closely related families to amplify across this subset.
> > > i.e. Some limited specificity of terminal sequence recognition by transposase. And families are related based on similarity of their terminal sequences
> > >
> > > My alternate hypothesis 2 - is that autonomous Helitrons across all families and expand them.

> > >
> > > HELP / ADVICE I SEEK FROM YOU
> > >

> > > 2. Should I use counts to counts comparison for the stats analysis

> > >
> > > 3. Does it make sense to analyze just one species at a time? In which case, it will be more or less like an Excel scatter plot with regression line and R2 value on it. Right?
> > >
> > > 4. OR  should I necessarily use as many species as possible? Is 12 a sufficient number? I can imagine a scenario where one Helitron cluster i.e. one of the 2709 families, shows high correlation between # autonomous and non-autonomous counts, across all 12 species. But is n=12 high enough to provide good p-value stats support for this?
> > >
> > > 5. I mentioned a LOT of the grid cells are zeroes. So it should be OK to remove cases where both the autonomous and non-autonomous counts = 0, since they should not alter the results, correct?
> > > Other than the obvious scenrario of
> > > # autonomous > 0, # non-autonomous > 0,
> > > you can also imagine cases where:
> > > # autonomous = 0, # non-autonomous > 0, and conversely
> > > # autonomous > 0, # non-autonomous = 0
> > > Therefore, will the analysis have to be performed in a special way to factor in these scenarios?

> > > Thank you!

Hi Anand,

Responses in-line...

Anand K S Rao wrote:
> Hi again Daniel,
>
> All important questions, please see my responses in-line.
>
> On Mon, Jun 8, 2015 at 5:04 PM, Daniel Fulop <dfulo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Anand,
> >
> > On second thought, in terms of adjusting for phylogenetic affect, perhaps I should've asked: How old are the 2079 TE families?  Are they homologous, i.e. do they all share a single origin for Eudicots and grasses, etc?
>
> I have not determined age of TEs,so I do not know the answer to this question. But I can say with reasonable certainty that there is way more stochasticity in the birth and death of TEs - especially non-autonomous, than classic genes for example. But you already know that. This TE class captures genes and gene fragments, which means on top of this stochasticity, is another layer of selection. So while closely related species will have a common origin of a small subset of TEs, I will expect divergence rates to be higher than for regular non-TE genes. At this point, I do not want to go into the annotation of TE contents, and I am happy with classifying them based on their terminal sequences... Does that answer these questions?

So, this sort of classification makes it so the TE families are typically only shared by somewhat near relatives, correct?  ...i.e. among grasses, or crucifers, etc

...and then for all other species the data entries are zero or NA because either that TE family isn't shared or is undetectable due to sequence divergence, correct?  In some sense I wouldn't call those "true" zeroes, because the TEs are potentially there yet classified under different families because the above distinction isn't made.  It's all okay, I'm just trying to understand your data and what's a proper way of analyzing it.

Given the above, I think naively using a zero-inflated model is the wrong choice.  If the data are cleaned up / reformatted to remove zeroes that could be due to non-detection due to sequence divergence, then any remaining zero inflation would be reasonable to model with a ZI-Poisson or a ZI-NB model.  It would be sensible to start with a non-ZI model and then add zero inflation (ZI) if needed.  After reformatting, the remaining zeroes would be e.g. for a family present in crucifers that was nevertheless not detected in 1 or a few crucifers.

All of this also complicates the question of adjusting for the effect of phylogeny, so it's best to leave that aside for now.  For the sake of brevity I won't get into the subtleties of it right now, but we could discuss it at a later time.  It also may okay to include it (again I won't get into the weeds), but I doubt it'll make any difference for other reasons...

>
>
> MCMCglmm is a contributed package, not base R.  It has good vignettes and documentation, but the learning curve can be a bit steep in terms of specifying priors  ...although the default priors often work quite well for simple models, which yours would be.
>

No.  MCMCglmm is a different package.  glmmadmb can fit count based models and even ZI count models (though it cannot, at least not without messing directly with ADMB, fit a phylogenetic effect) using maximum likelihood (i.e. not in a bayesian framework with priors, etc).

Hi Daniel,

Comment on Zero Inflation
A little more detail about how the families were created and populated with members.

The classification of TEs into families is based on clustering of 30bp 3' terminal sequences at 80% identity.
The 5' terminal is way more divergent, so cant be used. The internal sequences also are variant, because this class of TEs can pick up genes and gene fragments.....so much variation in internal region between terminals to be of real use...

Had I clustered at more stringent 90% sequence identity or less stringent 70% sequence identity, it would have resulted in more or fewer families, thereby changing how many zeroes are seen in the dataframe, starting the same TE counts for each genome. So yes, in some sense, the zeroes I see here reflects abundance within sub-groups, but this sub-grouping itself will have an effect on how the slices i.e. TE counts, are distributed.

Sharing TEs across distant or related species?
Yes, generally, I would expect that TEs are shared across close species. But that is not to say that they cannot be shared across a wider taxonomic range. This is complicated by the fact that some of these TEs actually contain or overlap with genes, that may have been selected for and retained! So I hesitate to give you a definitive answer, because I am not sure about the full picture.

When I looked to see how many families were shared across all 48 genomes, that answer is a bog fat zero.
In fact, the most number of genomes that any one TE family is found in is just 18. Not even close to 48.

But I have not looked at the distribution of these 18 to see if they are all present in one clade and absent from another, or if it is more random than that.....I should look at it...

Implementation
I suppose you were referring to this earlier: http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/MCMCglmm/MCMCglmm.pdf
So in terms of actually performing the analyses, do I need to perform one or more exploratory steps before choosing which approach to take? Or will it be OK to stick with the MCMCglmm right off the bat? Is there a good one that comes with this package you recommend I look at?

Thank you, Daniel.
- Anand

Or will it be OK to stick with the MCMCglmm right off the bat? This TE class captures genes and gene fragments, which means on top of this stochasticity, is another layer of selection. > > So, this sort of classification makes it so the TE families are typically only shared by somewhat near relatives, correct?  ...i.e. among grasses, or crucifers, etc

#' correlation matrix chart

#'

#' Visualization of a Correlation Matrix. On top the (absolute) value of the

#' correlation plus the result of the cor.test as stars. On bottom, the

#' bivariate scatterplots, with a fitted line

#'

#'

#' @param R data for the x axis, can take matrix,vector, or timeseries

#' @param histogram TRUE/FALSE whether or not to display a histogram

#' @param method a character string indicating which correlation coefficient

#'           (or covariance) is to be computed.  One of "pearson"

#'           (default), "kendall", or "spearman", can be abbreviated.

#' @param \dots any other passthru parameters into \code{\link{pairs}}

#' @note based on plot at

#' \url{http://addictedtor.free.fr/graphiques/sources/source_137.R}

#' @author Peter Carl

#' @seealso \code{\link{table.Correlation}}

###keywords ts multivariate distribution models hplot

#' @examples

#'

#' data(managers)

#' chart.Correlation(managers[,1:8], histogram=TRUE, pch="+")

#'

#' @export

chart.Correlation <-

function (R, histogram = TRUE, method=c("pearson", "kendall", "spearman"), ...)

{ # @author R Development Core Team

  # @author modified by Peter Carl

    # Visualization of a Correlation Matrix. On top the (absolute) value of the

    # correlation plus the result of the cor.test as stars. On botttom, the

    # bivariate scatterplots, with a fitted line

    x = checkData(R, method="matrix")

    if(missing(method)) method=method[1] #only use one

    # Published at http://addictedtor.free.fr/graphiques/sources/source_137.R

    panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", use="pairwise.complete.obs", method, cex.cor, ...)

    {

        usr <- par("usr"); on.exit(par(usr))

        par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))

        r <- cor(x, y, use=use, method=method) # MG: remove abs here

        txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]

        txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")

        if(missing(cex.cor)) cex <- 0.8/strwidth(txt)

        test <- cor.test(x,y, method=method)

        # borrowed from printCoefmat

        Signif <- symnum(test$p.value, corr = FALSE, na = FALSE,

                    cutpoints = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 1),

                    symbols = c("***", "**", "*", ".", " "))

        # MG: add abs here and also include a 30% buffer for small numbers

        text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex * (abs(r) + .3) / 1.3)

        text(.8, .8, Signif, cex=cex, col=2)

    }

    f <- function(t) {

    dnorm(t, mean=mean(x), sd=sd.xts(x) )

    }

    hist.panel = function (x, ...) {

        par(new = TRUE)

        hist(x,

             col = "light gray",

             probability = TRUE,

             axes = FALSE,

             main = "",

             breaks = "FD")

        lines(density(x, na.rm=TRUE),

              col = "red",

              lwd = 1)

        #lines(f, col="blue", lwd=1, lty=1) how to add gaussian normal overlay?

        rug(x)

      }

    # Draw the chart

    if(histogram)

        pairs(x, gap=0, lower.panel=panel.smooth, upper.panel=panel.cor, diag.panel=hist.panel, method=method, ...)

    else

        pairs(x, gap=0, lower.panel=panel.smooth, upper.panel=panel.cor, method=method, ...)

}

##Plotting my data to chart.correlation

## Correlation matrix with p-values. See http://goo.gl/nahmV for documentation of this function

cor.prob <- function (X, dfr = nrow(X) - 2) {

  R <- cor(X, use="pairwise.complete.obs")

  above <- row(R) < col(R)

  r2 <- R[above]^2

  Fstat <- r2 * dfr/(1 - r2)

  R[above] <- 1 - pf(Fstat, 1, dfr)

  R[row(R) == col(R)] <- NA

  R

}

## Use this to dump the cor.prob output to a 4 column matrix

## with row/column indices, correlation, and p-value.

## See StackOverflow question: http://goo.gl/fCUcQ

flattenSquareMatrix <- function(m) {

  if( (class(m) != "matrix") | (nrow(m) != ncol(m))) stop("Must be a square matrix.")

  if(!identical(rownames(m), colnames(m))) stop("Row and column names must be equal.")

  ut <- upper.tri(m)

  data.frame(i = rownames(m)[row(m)[ut]],

             j = rownames(m)[col(m)[ut]],

             cor=t(m)[ut],

             p=m[ut])

}

## get the CRG biomass data

##Mydata

Crgdata = read.table("C:/ CRGbiomassteena_redo1.txt", header=TRUE)

## use the path that your data file is located at

## In order to see if R is reading datacrgdata

crgdata

## You should see your data

# correlation matrix

cor(crgdata)

# correlation matrix with p-values

cor.prob(crgdata)

# "flatten" that table

flattenSquareMatrix(cor.prob(crgdata))

# plot the data

chart.Correlation(crgdata)

messages.body_plain:
When you put a pound sign (aka hastag aka #) in front of a line of code, it tells R to ignore that line. So this:

text(.8, .8, Signif, cex=cex, col=2)

will run and this:

#text(.8, .8, Signif, cex=cex, col=2)

will not.

Don't delete the txt line, you need it, it creates the R^2 numbers.

messages.body_plain:
I have this data frame:
output = structure(list(run = c(2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L), start = c(0L,
0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L), time = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 40
), N = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 0, 0), P = c(0, 2, 2, 4, 5, 4, 0,
0)), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"), row.names = c(NA,
-8L), .Names = c("run", "start", "time", "N", "P"), vars = list(
    run, start))

output
Source: local data frame [8 x 5]

  run start time N P
1   2     0    0 1 0
2   2     0    1 1 2
3   2     0    2 2 2
4   2     0    3 2 4
5   2     0    5 2 5
6   2     0    6 1 4
7   2     0    9 0 0
8   2     0   40 0 0

time represents time points where N and P change, but I want to expand this data frame to include all time points 0:40, and the values of N and P, even if they repeat. My first thought was to start by doing a join, like so:
library(dplyr)
output_expanded = output  %>%
  full_join(data.frame(run = .$run[1], start=.$start[1], time=0:max(.$time))) %>%
  arrange(time)
output_expanded
Source: local data frame [41 x 5]

   run start time  N  P

3    2     0    2  2  2

8    2     0    7 NA NA
9    2     0    8 NA NA
10   2     0    9  0  0
.. ...   ...  ... .. ..

This gives me a data frame with all the time points and NAs for N and P. But I want the N and P values to be the same as the previous non-NA value, like so:
   run start time  N  P
1    2     0    0  1  0
2    2     0    1  1  2
3    2     0    2  2  2

Any thoughts how to do this? I tried
output_expanded %>% mutate(N = ifelse(is.na <http://is.na>(N), lag(N), N)

but this doesn’t work because lag(N) is calculated for the whole vector at once rather than iteratively; it only fills in the first of each run of NA.

Here's a for loop approach that appears to do the trick (in this example).

library(plyr) # going old school Hadley

times <- 0:max(output$time)

for (i in times) {
  if (!(i %in% output$time)) {
    tmp <- output[i,]
    tmp$time <- i
    output <- rbind(output, tmp)
    output <- plyr::arrange(output, time)

}

Answering my own question: it looks like the zoo package has a function called na.locf(), for last observation carried forward. It does this:
v = c(1, 1, 2, NA, 3, NA, NA, 4)
zoo::na.locf(v)
[1] 1 1 2 2 3 3 3 4

So my solution is:
output_expanded = output  %>%
  full_join(data.frame(run = .$run[1], start=.$start[1], time=0:max(.$time))) %>%
  arrange(time) %>%
  mutate(N = zoo::na.locf(N), P = zoo::na.locf(P))
output_expanded

Voila!

messages.body_plain:
Complicatedly, but it manages to avoid loops in R. Here’s the source. It seems the internal function na.locf.0 has the important parts:
> na.locf.default
function (object, na.rm = TRUE, fromLast, rev, maxgap = Inf,
    rule = 2, ...)
{
    L <- list(...)
    if ("x" %in% names(L) || "xout" %in% names(L)) {
        if (!missing(fromLast)) {
            stop("fromLast not supported if x or xout is specified")
        }
        return(na.approx(object, na.rm = na.rm, maxgap = maxgap,
            method = "constant", rule = rule, ...))
    }
    na.locf.0 <- function(x) {
        L <- !is.na <http://is.na>(x)
        idx <- if (fromLast)
            rev(c(NA, rev(which(L)))[cumsum(rev(L)) + 1])
        else c(NA, which(L))[cumsum(L) + 1]
        na.index <- function(x, i) {
            L <- !is.na <http://is.na>(i)
            x[!L] <- NA
            x[L] <- coredata(x)[i[L]]
            x
        }
        xf <- na.index(x, idx)
        .fill_short_gaps(x, xf, maxgap = maxgap)
    }
    if (!missing(rev)) {
        warning("na.locf.default: rev= deprecated. Use fromLast= instead.")
        if (missing(fromLast))
            fromLast <- rev
    }
    else if (missing(fromLast))
        fromLast <- FALSE
    rev <- base::rev
    object[] <- if (length(dim(object)) == 0)
        na.locf.0(object)
    else apply(object, length(dim(object)), na.locf.0)
    if (na.rm)
        na.trim(object, is.na <http://is.na> = "all")
    else object
}
<environment: namespace:zoo>
> zoo:::.fill_short_gaps
function (x, fill, maxgap)
{
    if (maxgap <= 0)
        return(x)
    if (maxgap >= length(x))
        return(fill)
    naruns <- rle(is.na <http://is.na>(x))
    naruns$values[naruns$lengths > maxgap] <- FALSE
    naok <- inverse.rle(naruns)
    ifelse(naok, fill, x)
}
<environment: namespace:zoo>
​

messages.subject: Matrix syntax confusion
messages.subject_clean: Matrix syntax confusion
messages.body_plain:
Hey guys,

I'm just trying to figure out why this code renders the results it does:

First, just create a couple of vectors (representing views on social media pages, in this case) and put them into a matrix
# social data
linkedin <- c(16, 9, 13, 5, 2, 17, 14)
facebook <- c(17, 7, 5, 16, 8, 13, 14)
views <- matrix(c(linkedin, facebook), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

Then, try to answer the question of how often facebook views equals or exceeds twice the amount of linkedin views:
# How often does facebook equal or exceed linkedin times two?

sum(views[1, ] >= 2 * views[2, ]) # incorrect; outputs 1

sum(facebook >= 2*linkedin) # correct; outputs 2

Why does that first line of code output 1 instead of 2?  And why does it work just as well as the second line when I remove the multiplier?
# Take out the 2* multiplier and it works:

sum(views[1, ] >= views[2, ]) # correct; outputs 4

sum(facebook >= linkedin) # correct; outputs 4

Thanks!  I'm sure it's just a syntax issue.  But it made me curious because I can't figure out why the syntax is incorrect.  Adding parentheses didn't change anything.

Best,
Myfanwy

It's *very* difficult to proofread one's own work.  Our brains just
"fill in the blanks" for us.  I once had a "customer", a very bright
guy, who came to me with a problem.  I took a look at it for about
three seconds and noticed that he had transposed two letters, which I
pointed out to him.  That elicited the only F-bomb I had ever heard
from the guy (angry at himself, not at me).  He said he before coming
in to my office he had stopped in the hallway to make sure he hadn't
overlooked anything like that.  He had.

-- Mike

messages.subject: Pie chart slice customization
messages.subject_clean: Pie chart slice customization
messages.body_plain:
Is it possible to customize where I want the pie slices to be in this code?  I would like the "Carbon" fraction slice to be on the "positive X axis" of the circle - or to rephrase, horizontal on the right.  I want this slice to open up to another pie chart in my design program so it would be ideal to change it's location to the right instead up in the upper right quadrant.

library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

fraction <- c("Biomass", "Carbon","Water")
my_data <- data.frame(
  fraction = factor(fraction, fraction),
  percentage = c(13, 10, 77))
y_breaks <- cumsum(my_data$percentage) - my_data$percentage/2
y_labels <- c("Biomass","Water")
y_percentage = c(13, 10, 77)

p1 <- ggplot(my_data, aes(x = factor(1), y = percentage, fill = fraction)) +
  geom_bar(width = 1, colour = "black", stat = "identity") +
  guides(fill = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 1.70, y = y_breaks,
                label = y_labels, hjust = c(NA, NA, NA)), size = 7, family="Times") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 1.2, y = y_breaks, label = paste0(y_percentage, "%")),
            size = 7, family="Times", colour = c("black", "black", "black")) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("plum4", "grey","powderblue")) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_blank(),
        plot.margin = unit(c(0, 0, -0.5, 0),"cm"),
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank())

messages.body_plain:
The pdf() command tells R to open a PDF graphics device, that is, make a PDF file and write any graphics to that file rather than the screen. Until you call that command, R outputs graphics to the screen, instead. Here you call pdf() only before your last plotting command (plot(trunk$carbon~trunk$trunkdia)), but you have several plotting commands beforehand that are not being written to the file. You want to call pdf() before all of these, like so:
names(trunk)=c("trunkdia","carbon")
trunk$trunk2=(trunk$trunkdia)^2
trunk$trunkS=scale(trunk$trunkdia,scale=F)
trunk$trunkS2=(trunk$trunkS)^2
####### calculation of the coefficient
m=coef(lm(trunk$carbon ~ trunk$trunkdia + trunk$trunk2-1,trunk=trunk))
cint=confint(lm(trunk$carbon ~ trunk$trunkdia + trunk$trunk2-1,trunk=trunk))
####### your statistics
summary(lm(trunk$carbon~ trunk$trunkS + trunk$trunkS2,trunk=trunk))
########## plot of the quadratic regression + confidence interval
# quadratic
quadratic<-lm(trunk$carbon ~ trunk$trunkdia+I(trunk$trunkdia^2))
summary(quadratic)
cq = coef(quadratic)

pdf("Wood_Dia6.pdf", par(family="Times"))  ## <-- Calling pdf() before all the plotting commands, create a PDF file to write in

plot(trunk$carbon~ trunk$trunkdia,ylim=c(0,max(trunk$carbon)),xlim=c(0,max(trunk$trunkdia)), cex.axis=1.5, xlab="Trunk Diameter (mm)",  ylab=expression(Wood ~ C ~(kg ~ C ~ vine^{-1})), cex.lab=1.5, pch=20, cex=1,)  ## <-- Make the plot

curve(m[1]*x+m[2]*x*x,add=T)  ##                            <-- Add some curves
curve(cint[1,1]*x+cint[2,1]*x*x,add=T,lty=2,col=2)
curve(cint[1,2]*x+cint[2,2]*x*x,add=T,lty=2,col=2)
coefs <- coef(lm(trunk$carbon~ trunk$trunkS + trunk$trunkS2,trunk=trunk))
b0 <- round(coefs[1],2)
b1 <- round(coefs[2],2)
r2 <- round(summary(lm(trunk$carbon~ trunk$trunkS + trunk$trunkS2,trunk=trunk))$r.squared, 2)
eqn <- bquote(italic(y) == .(round(m[1],30))*italic(x) + .(round(m[2],30))*italic(x^2)  ~~~  r^2 == .(r2), options(digits=2))

text(1, 5.5, eqn, cex = 1, adj=c(0,0))   ## <-- Add the equation label

dev.off()  ## <-- Finish making the the plot, write it to the PDF file.
​

messages.body_plain:
You can change the margins of the plot with the mar argument of the par() function, which sets graphical parameters. par() should be run before your first plotting function, but after the pdf() command, as it sets up the plotting environment of the graphics device. The default margins are mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1, which are for bottom, left, top, and right margins, respectively, so you’ll want a larger second value, like so:
pdf('myfile.pdf')
par(mar = c(5.1, 5.1, 4.1, 2.1))
plot(...
etc.

The ?par help page gives an overview of graphical parameters.

For a general introduction to using R base plotting, our own Michael Koontz wrote a very good tutorial script <http://www.noamross.net/blog/2015/4/24/koontz-base-plotting.html>. Also very useful for things like this (layout, margins, etc.) is Chapter 3 of Paul Murrell’s R Graphics book <http://www.crcnetbase.com/doi/book/10.1201/9781420035025>. You should be able to access it from on campus or with the VPN.
​

messages.body_plain:
Greetings.  Last year I wrote (yet another) introduction to R to be
distributed as a handout for a class.  I've attached to this note the PDF
version of the document, as well as the (more-important) Rmarkdown file that
serves as the source.

Probably if you know much about R you won't find anything of interest in the
document, but it does contain information relevant to some of the questions
that have come up recently on this list.

The one, and possibly only, advantage to the document is that one can run all
of the associated R code very simply from RStudio (or Emacs), and that was the
intended modus operandi: the students would examine the code, run the code,
and grok the results.

Hence, the PDF version of the document gives an incomplete picture of the
contents.  (Note that many of the code chunks are marked with "eval=FALSE".)
You really have to run the code from the Rmd file to see the complete picture.

Some notes:

(1) The document was intended for students with some prior programming
background.  Some of the discussion is a little "geeky" for general use.

(2) The emphasis is on programming.

(3) There is some discussion of concepts related to R packages, but there
isn't much discussion of specific packages.

(4) There is a fair amount of discussion of graphics, but only about "base"
graphics.  No ggplot, for instance.

(5) I don't think there's any use of the Hadleyverse at all.  I don't recall
that this was a conscious omission.  You just have to stop writing at some
point.

As I said, I don't know how much use this will be to anybody, and my feelings
will not be hurt if y'all ignore it completely.

OTOH, if you *do* happen to look at some or all of the document and you find
errors, incomplete or confusing discussions, etc., please let me know.

-- Mike

messages.body_plain:
This seems like a reasonable approach if (a) you need to get something
out in a hurry and (b) you don't expect to have to repeat the task
many times.  The advantage to fiddling with the parameters in R (or
Python or ...) is that the program will always "remember" the right
steps to take to generate the image.  When I start hacking at things
with a mouse, I tend to forget to record the stuff I've done (hence,
have to  re-discover the next time).

-- Mike

> On Sun, Jun 14, 2015 at 7:05 PM, Noam Ross <noam...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> You can change the margins of the plot with the mar argument of the par()
>> function, which sets graphical parameters. par() should be run before your
>> first plotting function, but after the pdf() command, as it sets up the
>> plotting environment of the graphics device. The default margins are mar =
>> c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1, which are for bottom, left, top, and right margins,
>> respectively, so you’ll want a larger second value, like so:
>>
>> pdf('myfile.pdf')
>> par(mar = c(5.1, 5.1, 4.1, 2.1))
>> plot(...
>> etc.
>>
>> The ?par help page gives an overview of graphical parameters.
>>
>> For a general introduction to using R base plotting, our own Michael
>> Koontz wrote a very good tutorial script. Also very useful for things like
>> this (layout, margins, etc.) is Chapter 3 of Paul Murrell’s R Graphics book.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dorothy,

I'm not familiar with the package, but after reading through some of the documentation <http://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/pathview/inst/doc/pathview.pdf>, it seems that at the most basic level you want a column of data representing relative gene expression for many different genes between treatment conditions. In the example they give, it's microarray data, and "pair-wise gene expression changes between DCIS (disease) and HN (control) samples." If you're working with RNA-seq data, however, I'm guessing you'd want to use some of sort of metric like ratio of Fragments Per Kilobase of transcript per Million mapped reads (FPKM) between two samples.

Hopefully that gets you at least part of the way to your data import/set up.

>From there, the call to pathview() also seems to require the study species in question and the pathway of interest. I'm not sure what species you're working with, but I'm assuming it's important that you're working with a well-characterized pathway and using gene names that Pathview recognizes in order to get good results.

Hope that helps,
Evan

messages.subject_clean: Predict continuous response with categorical predictor variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am using glm to predict Weight_Gain by three predictor variables (two continuous, one categorical). For the two continuous variables, I can use the predict() to predict the response holding everything except my one independent variable of interest constant. For example:
TRat.min <- min(All.SRs.Head$TRat, na.rm = T)
TRat.max <- max(All.SRs.Head$TRat, na.rm = T)
TRat.seq <- seq(from=TRat.min,to=TRat.max,length.out=1000)

# make a new DF that varies only along the predictor of interest
newdf.TRat <- data.frame(TRat=TRat.seq,SL.YL="Season",Area=28.85)

#make a prediction, also outputting standard errors and converting those to 95% confidence limits
pred = predict(glm_model, newdata = newdf.TRat, terms = "response", se.fit=TRUE)
pred.mean <- pred$fit
pred.ci.low <- pred$fit-pred$se.fit*1.96
pred.ci.high <- pred$fit + pred$se.fit*1.96

However, I am not sure how to do that when I want to do something similar for a categorical predictor. For example, I would like to allow SL.YL (the categorical predictor) to vary between the two levels, and then predict the continuous response of Weight_Gain while holding Area and TRat constant at some median level.

Thank you for any leads!

Kristina
​

I might be totally wrong here, but I think it is actually quite easy. If you are only varying a categorical variable with two possible levels, your new data frame would only have two lines, one for each level of the factor. The rest of the values would be the median for that variable. Then you can use your same code with the "predict" function:
TRat.min <- min(All.SRs.Head$TRat, na.rm = T)
TRat.max <- max(All.SRs.Head$TRat, na.rm = T)
TRat.seq <- seq(from=TRat.min,to=TRat.max,length.out=1000)

# make a new DF that varies only along the predictor of interest
newdf.TRat <- data.frame(TRat=median(TRat),SL.YL= c("Season", "Yourotherfactorlevel"), Area=28.85)

pred = predict(glm_model, newdata = newdf.TRat, terms = "response", se.fit=TRUE)
pred.mean <- pred$fit
pred.ci.low <- pred$fit-pred$se.fit*1.96
pred.ci.high <- pred$fit + pred$se.fit*1.96

Somehow I feel like I am probably missing something though, since this seems too easy.

messages.body_plain:
Since your variable is a factor with two levels, you only need two lines in your data frame, one for each factor level. Use the two-line data frame to predict your continuous response.

SL.YL_seq <-levels(All.SRs.Head$SL.YL)
newdf.TRat <- data.frame(TRat=median(TRat),SL.YL= SL.YL_seq, Area=28.85)

pred = predict(glm_model, newdata = newdf.TRat, terms = "response", se.fit=TRUE)
pred.mean <- pred$fit
pred.ci.low <- pred$fit-pred$se.fit*1.96
pred.ci.high <- pred$fit + pred$se.fit*1.96

Does that make sense? If all the other predictor variables are held constant, you only need to predict the continuous response variable for the two different levels of the categorical variable.

With plotting it seems as though it's expecting a vector instead of a list, judging from the error.

messages.body_plain:
Kristina,

You're ending up with 2 point because that's all that you have in newdata, i.e. 2 rows for your 2 factor levels because you're holding everything else constant as Rosemary is pointing out.

To put it another way, your Weight_Gain response *does not* vary in a continuous manner with respect to your categorical predictor SL.YL, rather Weight_Gain varies in a discrete manner with respect to SL.YL.

If you wanted to end up with more than 2 points, you'd have to vary (at least one of) the other predictors as well.  You could do that by varying all your predictors with a call such as:

newdata <- expand.grid(TRat=TRat.seq, SL.YL=SL.YL.seq, Area=Area.seq)  ...where each "seq" is a sequence of values from min to max or the levels of a factor, respectively.  This would give you a data.frame with all of the combinations of the supplied numeric and and factor vectors.

However, it seems like you want to visualize each predictor's effect separately, in which case 2 points is all *you should* end up with for a 2-level categorical predictor such as SL.YL.

Seconding Rosemary's request, attaching some code and data would help us help you to troubleshoot.  ...that would also help us help you with plotting these categorical predictions.  FWIW, I would use ggplot2 for plotting as it handles categorical axes without any extra complication.

messages.subject: July 6-7 workshop in R, git, and shell
messages.subject_clean: July 6-7 workshop in R, git, and shell
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

See below an announcement for a 2-day workshop I'll be teaching along with Easton White and Titus Brown in July.  The topics will be data processing, plotting, and making reproducible reports in R, using version control to organize your analyses, and automating tedious tasks using using the shell.

This workshop is aimed at those with a little bit of experience with R but aiming to make their work more efficient, organized, reproducible and sharable. If you attended the Data Carpentry workshop this winter, this would be a good follow-up. We encourage people to sign up with a colleague or group from your lab.

This is open to all and will probably fill up fast! E-mail me if you have questions.

Noam

---------- Forwarded message ---------
From: C. Titus Brown <ctb...@ucdavis.edu>
Date: Mon, Jun 22, 2015 at 8:16 AM
Subject: [dib-training] Software Carpentry workshop, July 6-7, at UC Davis.
To: <dib-tr...@lists.idyll.org>

Workshop announcement: Software Carpentry.

Who: Noam Ross, Steve Easton, and C. Titus Brown (organizer).
When: July 6 and 7, 2015
Times: 9am-5pm on both days
Where: 1041 Valley Hall, UC Davis campus.

Description:

Software Carpentry's mission is to help scientists and engineers get
more research done in less time and with less pain by teaching them
basic lab skills for scientific computing. This hands-on workshop will
cover basic concepts and tools, including program design, version
control, data management, and task automation. Participants will be
encouraged to help one another and to apply what they have learned to
their own research problems.

Topics covered will include command line, git, and R.

More at:
http://dib-lab.github.io/2015-07-06-ucdavis/

This free workshop is open to everyone, including graduate students,
postdocs, staff, faculty, and the broader Bay Area community (incuding
IT and biotech). We have reserved space for UC Davis VetMed
affiliates; please contact the organizer if you are affiliated with
the SVM.

We especially encourage people to come with one or more colleagues
from their lab or research group!

More at:
http://dib-lab.github.io/2015-07-06-ucdavis/

Registration link:
https://www.eventbrite.com/e/software-carpentry-registration-17480416396

----

This workshop is hosted by the Lab for Data Intensive Biology as part of
their training program; see

http://dib-training.readthedocs.org/en/pub/

for more information.

_______________________________________________
dib-training mailing list
dib-tr...@lists.idyll.org
http://lists.idyll.org/listinfo/dib-training

Some folks on this list may be interested in the just-announced Mozilla Fellowships for Science.  These are 1-year fellowships for early-career researchers (graduate students, postdocs and project scientists) interested in working on open science, code and data sharing, and training.

Details below and at https://www.mozillascience.org/fellows
---

# Fellows | Mozilla Science Lab

Are you a champion of open science and open data? Mozilla is seeking researchers eager to advance openness in science and data within their institutions.

Call for fellows open until** August 14, 2015 at 11:59PM EDT**.  Apply at https://www.mozillascience.org/fellows.

The Mozilla Fellowships for Science present a unique opportunity for researchers who want to influence the future of open science and data sharing within their communities.

We're looking for researchers with a passion for open source and data sharing, already working to shift research practice to be more collaborative, iterative and open. Fellows will spend 10 months as community catalysts at their institutions, mentoring the next generation of open data practitioners and researchers and building lasting change in the global open science community.

Throughout their fellowship year, chosen fellows will receive training and support from Mozilla to hone their skills around open source and data sharing. They will also craft code, curriculum and other learning resources that help their local communities learn open data practices, and teach forward to their peers.

### EXPECTATONS

Fellows will:

* champion change within their university around open source and data sharing,
* create code, curriculum and other learning resources that help others learn open data practices,
* participate in Mozilla workweeks, trainings and community events (MozFest, code sprints, study groups, community events, project calls, etc.),
* participate and help lead regular community calls,
* serve as mentors and leaders within their communities,
* communicate and share openly their work on an ongoing basis (e.g., through GitHub repositories, scholarly preprints and blog posts).
* **Note:** Fellows are encouraged to continue their personal research for up to 20% of their time during the course of their fellowship (i.e., one day a week). Fellowship applicants must have buy in from their supervisors in advance, and include supervisors' contact information on the application. Advisers will be interviewed separately should applicants move on to the second round, and their support will be a critical consideration for acceptance of fellows.

### STIPEND AND FINANCIAL BENEFITS

The Fellowships are designed to allow for flexibility for both Fellows and their families. The standard fellowship offers a stipend of $60,000 USD, paid in 10 monthly installments. Fellows are responsible for remitting all applicable taxes and other government payments as required.

To help offset cost of living, the fellowship also provides supplements for childcare and health insurance, and helps pay for research/equipment and books. The fellowship also covers the costs of required travel for fellowship activities.

Fellows will receive:

* A stipend of $60,000 USD, paid in 10 monthly installments.
* One-time health insurance supplement for Fellows and their families, ranging from $3,500 for single Fellows to $7,000 for a couple with two or more children.
* One-time childcare allotment for families with children of up to $6,000.
* Allowance of up to $3,000 towards the purchase of laptop computer, digital cameras, recorders and computer software; fees for continuing studies or other courses, research fees or payments, to the extent related to the fellowship.
* All approved fellowship trips – domestic and international – are covered in full.

### ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA

* Fellows must be
    * Currently working at a research institution in the US, UK or Canada.
    * Currently an early-career researcher (i.e, graduate students, post-docs, research scientists, lecturers)
    * Specializing in the life sciences or natural sciences.
    * Able to travel.
    * Supported by their supervisors. As fellows will be based at their home institutions, please note that a letter of support from their supervisor is mandatory for consideration.
    * Have experience participating in open communities.

Call for fellows open until** August 14, 2015 at 11:59PM EDT**

messages.subject: Creating a Cumulative average / moving average
messages.subject_clean: Creating a Cumulative average / moving average
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am having difficulties finding a way to calculate a cumulative average. I am working with education data where I have one row per student per term, the units completed and the GPA for that term. The data is unbalanced in that not all students have the same number of terms. I would like to create a cumulative GPA per student per term. Here is a minimal working example. I am not sure how to go about calculating wtd.gpa[j] <- units[1]*gpa[1] + units[2]*gpa[2] + ... + units[j]*gpa[j]  for each student i from term 1 through j_i without writing some sort of loop. I'm hoping for a simple solution like cumsum().

# Set up fake data set: GPA and units data per student-per term
library(dplyr)
d <- data.frame(id = seq(1:5), maxterm = sample(1:8, size=5, replace=TRUE), n=1)
d <- d[rep(d$id, d$maxterm),]
d <- d %>% group_by(id) %>% mutate(nterm=cumsum(n))
d$gpa   <- runif(d$n,1,4)
d$units <- floor(rnorm(d$n, 10, 3))
d <- d %>% group_by(id) %>% mutate(cum.units = cumsum(units))
d$n <- d$maxterm <- NULL
d

Thanks,

-Robin​

Robin Jeffries, DrPH
Assistant Professor
Department of Mathematics and Statistics
California State University Chico
Holt 216
530-898-5767
rjef...@csuchico.edu
www.norcalbiostat.com <http://www.norcalbiostat.com>

messages.body_plain:
Based on Brandon's code I think this might do want you want:

d %>%
  mutate(score = gpa * units) %>%
  mutate(cum.score = cumsum(score)) %>%
  mutate(term.gpa = cum.score/cum.units)

# outputs:
   id nterm      gpa units cum.units    score cum.score term.gpa
1   1     1 3.886022    11        11 42.74625  42.74625 3.886022
2   1     2 2.893880     9        20 26.04492  68.79116 3.439558
3   1     3 2.075634    13        33 26.98324  95.77440 2.902255
4   2     1 2.995411     7         7 20.96787  20.96787 2.995411

Hope that helps,
Patrick

messages.body_plain:
Excellent! Thanks Patrick and Brandon!

FWIW you can combine all variables created into a single mutate statement.

d %>%
  mutate(score = gpa * units,
         cum.score = cumsum(score),
         term.gpa = cum.score/cum.units)​

-Robin

messages.subject: Helpers for Tuesday R/git/shell workshop
messages.subject_clean: Helpers for Tuesday R/git/shell workshop
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We're looking for a few helpers for next week's workshop on R, git, and the shell (https://dib-lab.github.io/2015-07-06-ucdavis/).  The workshop is sold out, but we are looking for a few helpers who can help answer questions and help students deal with programming/IT snafus during the interactive sessions. Expertise in all these topics is not needed - helpers will mostly be answering very basic questions and providing an extra set of eyes on students' code.

If you're at all interested in Software Carpentry <http://software-carpentry.org/> and possibly becoming an instructor or just learning some of SWC's pedagogical approach, this is a great opportunity.

Please let me know if you are interested and if you have any questions.

 - Noam
